hints: Focus on what thermal cracking really does, it breaks long C-C bonds to make smaller molecules with the same total atoms.
Count carbons first, oct-1-ene has 8 carbons, so any small 2, 3 or 4 carbon fragment can fit as long as the other fragment makes up the rest.
Check hydrogen balance too, an alkene feed can give a mixture of alkenes, alkanes and even dienes as long as C and H totals still add to C8H16.
walkthrough:
**Recall what cracking produces**

Cracking breaks a C-C single bond in a long chain. For an alkane it typically gives a shorter alkane plus a shorter alkene. For an alkene feed it is more flexible and can give alkenes, alkanes and dienes.

Starting molecule:
$$\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 = \text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}$$

**Test the simple alkenes W and X**

Ethene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$, and propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$, are classic cracking products. Breaking the long chain can easily leave a C2 or C3 alkene fragment.

Example:
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$$
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_6 + \text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$$

**Test the alkane Y**

Do not assume cracking of an alkene gives only alkenes. Hydrogen atoms redistribute, so an alkane like propane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, can form alongside a more unsaturated fragment.

Example balanced split:
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + \text{C}_5\text{H}_8$$

**Test the diene Z**

Buta-1,3-diene, $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}=\text{CH}_2$, has formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_6$. Paired with butane, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$, the totals balance perfectly.

Check atoms:
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_6 + \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$$
Carbon: 4 + 4 = 8, Hydrogen: 6 + 10 = 16. So all four compounds W, X, Y and Z are possible.

options.A: Correct. W and X are small alkenes formed by chain cleavage, Y is a small alkane formed with hydrogen redistribution, and Z is a diene formed alongside an alkane. All balance to C8H16, so all four can be obtained.
options.B: Incorrect. This correctly includes W, X and Y but wrongly excludes Z. Many students think only mono-alkenes form, but a diene plus an alkane is a valid balanced cracking pair for an alkene feed.
options.C: Incorrect. This correctly includes W, X and Z but wrongly excludes Y. Many students think cracking an alkene cannot give an alkane, but hydrogen redistribution means alkanes like propane are normal cracking products.
options.D: Incorrect. This includes only the two simple alkenes. It is the trap of thinking cracking gives alkenes only, forgetting that alkanes and dienes also appear to keep the C and H atom totals balanced.
